field.p: (Originally posted by KI6UGB / Jim Robison, KJ6MRV, on January 26, 2014)

Folks, I need some advice. I'm looking for a mobile antenna for my Yaesu FT-2900. I have been using 38" mag mounts and the antenna keeps hitting low trees. A 19" model would be better, but what will that do to my range? Any suggestions?

field.name: content
field.p: (Originally posted by KZ6T Charlie, September 22, 2013)
Hi Jim, I do have some experience with trees and antennas so here is my 2 cents.

Before you make a change, what is your mag mount mounted to? Do you have enough ground plane area to support a 1/4 wave? In my current Jeep situation, my antenna mount is essentially on the end of a mast that has virtually no ground plane area. A 1/2 wave antenna works great there, but a 1/4 wave is almost useless. So before you make the change, make sure you have enough ground plane. 1/4 wave in every direction will give decent results.

Are you still apt to hit branches with the 1/4 wave? If so, those short antennas don't bend nearly as much as the longer ones. If using a rigid NMO mount you might end up bending some sheet metal as well.

So back to your basic questions. I had very good luck with a Comet (now NGC) B-10 when it was mounted to the top of my van. It's quite short, only 12 inches, but works as both a 2m and 70cm antenna. That's the good part - the down side is there is virtually no gain to speak of, and it does need a ground plane. If I put it on my Jeep mount, it's a little better than a dummy load. I think Doug KF6LMB is using the same on top of his pickup. When I had it mounted on the van, I could hit any repeater in this area - Santa Rosa to Vacaville and Novato with 50 watts. Not nearly as far as a 1/2 wave with gain. A 1/2 wave on the same mount will get me into the Palo Alto repeater from Santa Rosa using 50 watts.
I do have a spare 1/4 wave mag mount that I won in the SCRA raffle that you are welcome to borrow as a comparison test between your 1/2 wave and a 1/4 wave before you go drilling any holes.
Charlie... KZ6T

field.p: (Originally posted by jim_robison, September 22, 2013)

Charlie, thanks for the thinking points. I will be mounting it on my Volvo wagon, so I guess the ground plane is as big as most SUVs, though not as big as an American van. Thank you for the loan offer. I have a mag mount, I just don't know what to stick in it.

An example of its use: above Nice on the hill, I contacted Charlie on the old English Hill antenna in Sebastopol with 60 watts. Same story contacting Mt Diablo, from up at Loon Lake 30 miles east of Georgetown, or 50 miles east of Auburn. This may be the loaner that Charlie has to loan to you. Good luck, KF6LMB

field.name: content
field.p: (Originally posted by Bob KG6ZDN, September 23, 2013)

Hi Jim, just a note of caution - I think that not all mag mounts will be tuned for all antennas, they have a matching coil built in to both couple to the ground plane and match the antenna. For a proper match and best results, be sure to use one designed for the antenna being used (one designed for a 5/8 wave antenna will differ from one designed for a 1/4 wave, etc.)
Good luck, 73, Bob KG6ZDN

field.name: content
field.p: (Originally posted by Brian, N6IIY, September 23, 2013)

Hi Bob, this might be the case if you are using a mag mount with a non-standard interface, meaning the mag mount was intended to be no more than part of a complete antenna system, not a separate product.
But all mag mounts I've seen sold as mag mounts using standard interfaces such as SO-239 or NMO can accommodate virtually any antenna with the proper connector.

I have used NMO mounts on my vehicles (both permanent and mag mounts) and have freely interchanged between 5/8 wave and 1/4 wave antennas with no ill effects. I have 1/4 wave antennas on the permanent mounts since that allows me to put the vehicles in the garage, but if I know I'll be somewhere a little extra oomph will help, I swap in the 5/8 wave once I'm out of the garage.
The 5/8 wave antennas I've used have their loading coil in their bases, between the NMO mount and the whip.
73, Brian, N6IIY

field.name: content
field.p: (Originally posted by NH7X on October 12, 2014)
Share your tips and tricks here.

Need a way to carry and dispense paracord without it kinking? Take a 1.25 liter plastic soft drink bottle, wash and dry it, then drill a 3/32 hole in the cap (deburr it). Feed 100 feet of unrolled paracord into the bottle, rattling it to push the cord to the bottom. Thread the loose end through the cap for storage in your trunk. Not as fast as using a reel, but it stores nicely and keeps the cord clean.

field.name: content
field.p: (Originally posted by KI6UGB on April 13, 2016)

Tip for winding wire antennas for storage: use a kite reel (available on Amazon for under $10). Remove the kite twine and cut a notch where it guides onto the spool, then drill a hole in the reel to feed wire onto it. The kite reel's folding handle and ratchet stop make it convenient. 75 feet of End Fed antenna wire wound on the reel stores well - this method keeps wire smooth without kinking, and works well for portable radial wires too.

field.name: content
field.p: (Originally posted by NH7X on March 8, 2015)
Undocumented FTM-400 feature - Cross Band Repeat. Yaesu left this out of the user manual, but the radio actually supports it.

Entering cross-band mode: Turn the APRS modem off. Set a UHF frequency in either the upper or lower display (VFO or memory). Set a VHF frequency in the other display (VFO or memory). Turn the FTM-400 off. Press and hold the lower 3 buttons to the right of the display, then press the power button. "X-BAND Repeater" will show between the upper and lower frequency displays if it worked.

Exiting cross-band mode: Turn the FTM-400 off. Press and hold the lower 3 buttons to the right of the display, then press the power button again. "X-BAND Repeater" will no longer be displayed. Return the frequencies to your preferences, and turn the APRS modem back on if you run APRS.

field.name: content
field.p: (Originally posted by Fred AE6SF on August 9, 2016)

The standard is "Red Right, Tongue Top." Anderson Powerpole connectors (PP15, PP30, PP45) are used for 12VDC systems - black is negative, red is positive. Contact size depends on wire gauge: PP15 for 18-16 AWG, PP30 for 14-12 AWG, PP45 for 10 AWG. Crimping is preferred over soldering, though cyanoacrylate glue works to bond the housings together.

When learning Morse Code, pangrams (sentences using all 26 letters of the alphabet) are handy for practicing sending and receiving. The classic one: "The quick brown fox jumps over a lazy dog."
A few more, by character count:

ul.li: (31) The five boxing wizards jump quickly.
(32) Pack my box with five dozen liquor jugs.
(35) The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog.
(41) A large fawn jumped quickly over white zinc boxes.
(44) Five or six big jet planes zoomed quickly by the tower.
(47) My grandfather picks up quartz and valuable onyx jewels.
(48) Fred specialized in the job of making very quaint wax toys.
(48) Sixty zippers were quickly picked from the woven jute bag.
(49) A quick movement of the enemy will jeopardize six gunboats.
(49) All questions asked by five watch experts amazed the judge.
(49) How razorback jumping frogs can level six piqued gymnasts.
(50) We promptly judged antique ivory buckles for the next prize.

Considering a Kenwood TM-V71A 144/440 MHz dual-band mobile transceiver for my truck - 50 watts, 1000 memory channels, EchoLink capability, true dual receive. Is this a good entry-level choice, or overkill? Open to other recommendations, and looking for antenna suggestions too.

field.name: content
field.p: (Originally posted by Scott, KJ6QIQ, on October 2, 2020)

That Kenwood is a great radio - I use one regularly for 2m contacts, local nets, and packet work. Easy to program by hand without special software, though you'll want to assign a hot key for mic-keypad frequency entry. I've used radios from all the major manufacturers and the Kenwood's display is one of the clearer ones. For installation, if you're mounting the main body under or behind the seat, consider an external speaker at the back of the unit - a compact Uniden speaker aimed the right direction helps a lot with volume.

field.name: content
field.p: (Originally posted by Scott, KJ6QIQ, on January 23, 2021)

Trying to power LED closet lights from a LiFePO4 battery instead of the original AC-to-DC power supply. They work fine on the original supply (12V, 1500mA), but on the 14V battery they cycle on and off every 1-2 seconds, even with the motion sensor covered.
Is the 14V vs 12V difference causing this? Would a buck converter set to 12V fix it?

field.name: content
field.p: (Originally posted by Fred AE6SF on January 23, 2021)
Would steer away from a cheap buck converter - they can generate RF noise. A quieter option: drop about 2V using four silicon diodes in series.

Also worth checking: whether the battery's output voltage is dropping or fluctuating, whether it's actually fully charged, and whether its battery management system might be shutting things down under load. What's the current draw you need?

record.field: Do I need to ground my mag mount antenna if I use it for a base station?

field.name: content
field.p: (Originally posted by KN6NOT on April 23, 2023)

Have an outdoor mag mount antenna on an oil pan as a ground plane, feeding coax into my radio indoors. Considering putting in a bulkhead connector through the wall. Do I need grounding and lightning arrestors here, especially since I'm using a small PVC pipe "tower" to stay under the radar of HOA antenna restrictions?

record.field: Do I need to ground my mag mount antenna if I use it for a base station?

field.name: content
field.p: (Originally posted by WB6FRZ on April 26, 2023)

The "ground plane" on your mag mount is for RF impedance matching, not safety grounding - two different things. Earth ground (for dissipating a static/lightning charge via an arrestor) is separate from safety ground (recommended for tower installs, and on the technician exam). Most local amateur stations don't have either system and generally get by fine, though a lightning arrestor can help with a nearby strike.
Would suggest a copper-coated ground rod (~$20), and definitely use Coax Seal around your connections plus a drip loop to keep moisture out.

field.p: (Originally posted by Francis, KB7IP, on May 2, 2024)
Any suggestions for flooring in the shack? It'll be used for radio operations, repairs, and building, with a dedicated room and a workbench.
Options I'm considering:
Thanks & 73, Francis, KB7IP

field.name: content
field.p: (Originally posted by Bradley, KC6EOA, on May 10, 2024)
Hey Francis, a few thoughts. I've got wood flooring in my shack (office) and it works fine - easy to clean, dark colored, and my office chair rolls on it just fine.

With vinyl or carpet, watch out for a dropped soldering iron - it'll melt through those fast. Wood will burn too, but ceramic tile won't. Carpet also tends to make a room dustier, which isn't great with radios and other gear around - a throw rug for the dog is fine though.

Ceramic tile has grout lines, and chair wheels don't roll smoothly over them. Something without grout lines or depressions is easier to sweep and vacuum. Lighter flooring shows dirt sooner, but makes it easier to spot anything you drop.
Hope that helps, have fun with it. Bradley, KC6EOA
